extracted.intended_audience: law students, lawyers, First Amendment advocates, policy researchers, and general readers interested in internet censorship and constitutional law
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the constitutionality of state statutes regulating online adult content (labeling, registries, ISP filtering) under U.S. constitutional doctrines (First, Fourteenth Amendments, Commerce Clause), standing rules, and injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holding: protection for posting constitutionally protected adult content
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals cannot be prosecuted for posting constitutionally protected content for adults on general-access websites. They are not required by the Utah law to label such content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Dee Benson's May 15, 2012 declaratory judgment: individuals and service providers could not be prosecuted under Section 1206 nor subject to civil or criminal penalties under Section 1233 for failing to filter, block, or label constitutionally protected adult material on general-access sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: HB 260 — adult content registry and ISP/provider obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: House Bill 260 required the Utah Attorney General to maintain an 'adult content registry' of websites deemed 'harmful to minors' and required ISPs to block access or provide filtering software for these websites; it also required Utah ISPs to properly label or block their content, with criminal and civil penalties for failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill's provisions included creating a registry to identify 'harmful' sites, mandating ISP filtering/blocks, and imposing labeling obligations with penalties—these procedural requirements were the core statutory mechanisms challenged in the suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5: extension of state 'harmful to minors' law to Internet content providers and ISPs
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 sought to extend the existing Utah law on materials harmful to minors (Utah Code § 76-10-1206) to internet content providers and ISPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs specifically challenged this territorial/applicability expansion as part of the facial constitutional attack—whether statutes that previously targeted traditional distributors may be applied to online actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 9: Mandatory labeling provision (compelled labeling of content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 9 (the Mandatory Labeling provision) stated that Utah-based content providers were required to label their content, and imposed criminal penalties for failing to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs characterized this as compelled speech; Count 6 of the complaint alleged Section 9 violated the First Amendment. The court's order later found providers could not be penalized for failing to label constitutionally protected material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 2: creation of an 'adult content registry' by the Attorney General
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2 mandated the creation of an adult content registry by the Attorney General, consisting of a list of websites identified as containing material 'harmful to minors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The registry was the statutory mechanism the State said would narrow the law's reach and facilitate ISP filtering; plaintiffs argued such centralized identification and listing raised First Amendment and procedural due process concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 8: requirement that ISPs block access to registry-listed websites
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 8 correspondingly required ISPs to block access to websites that were listed in the adult content registry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges questioned the feasibility and constitutional implications of compelling ISPs to block registry-listed sites, including effects on non-requesting customers and interstate commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4: ISP obligation to block or restrict access to 'pornographic material' as determined by customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 required ISPs to block or restrict access to 'pornographic material' as determined by their customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs argued that technical realities of the Internet make individualized blocking difficult and that customer-determined blocking could result in inconsistent and overbroad restriction across networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 7: broad requirement that ISPs restrict access to material 'harmful to minors'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7 broadly required ISPs to restrict access to material 'harmful to minors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad, potentially vague mandate was challenged on First Amendment and due process grounds for overbreadth and lack of clear procedural safeguards for providers and users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count 1: Violation of adults' First and Fourteenth Amendment rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The law was alleged to be unconstitutional 'on its face' because it imposed unfair restrictions and burdens upon constitutionally protected speech between adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This facial challenge asserts the statute's text and structure burden protected adult-to-adult speech; analysis requires examination of overbreadth and the application of appropriate constitutional standards (e.g., strict scrutiny if content-based).

rubrics_metrics.name: Count 2: Violation of minors' First and Fourteenth Amendment rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The law was alleged to prevent minors from lawfully accessing content protected by the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims concerning minors require balancing protection interests with minors' rights; precedents (e.g., Ginsberg) allow some regulation with different standards, but application to the internet raises distinct issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count 3: Prior restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs alleged the law imposed a prior restraint by depriving plaintiffs of their ability to access and publish content on the Internet that was protected by the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior restraint doctrine is a high-bar constitutional rule; plaintiffs argued that registry/labeling/blocking schemes functioned as pre-publication restraints on speech or access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count 4: Inadequate procedural protections (Due Process)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law was alleged to lack adequate procedural protections for ISPs and other organizations under the Fourteenth Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural-due-process concerns included inadequate notice, definitionless listings, or insufficient review mechanisms for sites placed on a registry or subject to blocking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count 5: Violation of anonymous communication and access rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The law was alleged to violate the right to communicate and access information anonymously by requiring identification as an adult to access certain content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs argued mandatory identity-verification requirements chill speech and anonymity rights protected under the First and Fourteenth Amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count 6: Compelled speech (labeling) violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs alleged Section 9 compelled Utah-based content providers to label their speech as 'adult content' in violation of the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compelled-speech doctrine protects speakers from government-mandated messages/labels; plaintiffs argued mandatory labeling was an unconstitutional compulsion. The court's order rejected enforcement of such penalties against providers for constitutionally protected content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count 7: Commerce Clause violation (interstate commerce impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs alleged the Act violated the Commerce Clause by subjecting ISPs to 'inconsistent regulations' that impacted out-of-state users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Web-based regulation can implicate dormant Commerce Clause concerns when state rules affect interstate data flows or impose burdens on out-of-state commerce; plaintiffs cited conflicting regimes in other states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standing to challenge the statute
rubrics_metrics.description: The State moved to dismiss for lack of standing; the court found that while the majority of plaintiffs had standing, some plaintiffs (e.g., The King's English bookstore) did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing is a threshold requirement: plaintiffs must show concrete, particularized injury, causation, and redressability. The court's analysis separated which organizational and individual plaintiffs met those criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict scrutiny standard for speech restrictions affecting adults
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs argued that under strict scrutiny the infringement of adults' First and Fourteenth Amendment rights was not justified by a compelling government purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict scrutiny requires the government to show a compelling interest and that the statute is narrowly tailored to achieve that interest by the least restrictive means; the State sought to argue narrow tailoring via the registry/filtering design.

rubrics_metrics.name: State's asserted compelling interest and narrow tailoring defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The State argued the law was vital to apprehend sexual predators and protect minors, and that the registry/tagging system made the law narrower and therefore permissible under strict scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State relied on precedents (Sable Communications v. FCC, Ginsberg v. New York) to assert a compelling interest in protecting minors and showed the registry/tagging was intended to focus restrictions; constitutional analysis assesses whether such measures are actually narrowly tailored and not overbroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical realities of the Internet as a feasibility and overbreadth argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs argued that because of the 'technical realities' of the Internet, large ISPs would find it difficult to restrict access for one set of customers without restricting access across the network and to non-requesting customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both a practical and constitutional argument: technological impossibility or high cost of selective filtering can make statutory aims impracticable and increase risk of overinclusive suppression of lawful speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent: other federal and state cases striking down similar laws (Reno v. ACLU, Pappert, Nitke, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complaint and briefing cited multiple cases in which courts struck down laws applying criminal penalties for distributing harmful materials to minors on the Internet (e.g., Reno v. ACLU), as well as district-court decisions invalidating state ISP-restriction laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These precedents form the doctrinal backdrop: courts have repeatedly found broad internet-targeted restrictions problematic under the First Amendment; assessing a new statute requires comparing it to controlling precedent and analogues.
